query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the high‐density Ta in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with the lower‐density element Nb will reduce the overall density without sacrificing the high room‐temperature and elevated‐temperature (≈1000 °C) mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Substitute Ta with Nb to obtain the HfMoNbTiZr alloy (i.e. fix the composition by replacing Ta with Nb, keeping the other elements constant).
generation.conditions: Evaluate the alloy under similar processing (as‐cast state) and testing conditions as the baseline – specifically, mechanical testing at room temperature and around 1000 °C under compressive (or tensile) loading regimes comparable to those reported for HfMoTaTiZr.
generation.structural_mediator: The BCC solid solution microstructure and the underlying dislocation-based strengthening mechanisms that are preserved after elemental substitution.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a considerably lower density (~8.57 g/cm³) compared to Ta (~16.65 g/cm³); by replacing Ta with Nb, the average atomic mass of the alloy is reduced while retaining a similar atomic size and chemical compatibility. This maintains the solid solution strengthening and high-temperature stability (via a BCC structure) that provide high yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy (HfMoNbTiZr) is predicted to have a reduced density (estimated average around 8.6–8.7 g/cm³) while retaining comparable room‐temperature yield strength (on the order of 1350 MPa) and elevated‐temperature strength (yield strength above 800 MPa near 1000 °C) relative to the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and its known mechanical performance at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The performance is assessed under ambient conditions and at approximately 1000 °C, with standard mechanical loading (compression or tension) similar to previously reported tests.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding a possible modest reduction in yield strength or slight adjustments in ductility compared to HfMoTaTiZr; however, prior evidence suggests that the Nb substitution may even improve ductility without greatly compromising strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys using the same casting procedure: one set of the baseline as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr and one set with Ta fully replaced by Nb (HfMoNbTiZr). Measure and compare the density via Archimedes method, and perform standardized compressive (or tensile) tests at room temperature and around 1000 °C to evaluate yield strength, ductility, and ultimate strength.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower density than the baseline (e.g., density reduction of at least ~1.5–2 g/cm³) or if its mechanical properties at room temperature or at ≈1000 °C fall below acceptable thresholds (significantly lower yield strength or ductility compared to HfMoTaTiZr), then the hypothesis is falsified.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
